claims.text: Machine-learning-driven optimization of multiphase microstructures enables concurrent improvement of strength and ductility in conventional metallic systems.
The initial conventional metallic material has a homogeneous microstructure.
Strength and ductility are inversely related in the initial material.
Machine-learning algorithms can use alloy-composition and processing data to design multiphase microstructures.
Phase volume fraction, interphase spacing, and heat-treatment parameters can be tuned to produce bimodal or gradient structures.
A heat-treatment range of approximately 600–700°C with suitable holding times is relevant to the proposed optimization.
The optimized microstructure comprises fine, high-strength phases embedded in a ductile matrix.
The optimized microstructure has controlled interphase spacing and phase distribution.
The hard phase increases strength through load bearing.
The hard phase increases strength by obstructing dislocation motion.
The ductile phase promotes strain accommodation.
Combining hard and ductile phases reduces the conventional strength–ductility trade-off.
The optimized material will have greater yield strength than the homogeneous baseline.
The optimized material will have greater tensile strength than the homogeneous baseline.
The optimized material will have greater ductility than the homogeneous baseline.
Traditional strengthening methods typically reduce ductility.
Concurrent improvement may occur only within narrow ranges of phase fraction, interphase spacing, and thermal-processing conditions.
The effectiveness of the machine-learning approach depends on the quality and diversity of its input data.
